object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account; everything (subscriptions, billing) hangs off it. Treated as the 'customer' in the system.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six-digit sequential identifier for an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product sold by the company, e.g. CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.
Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact -- the plan code that says what a customer pays and how often; generates invoice lines.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a price plan, e.g. CORE-MO-49.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: What the customer gets: the feature bundle -- seats, API access, SSO -- shown on the pricing page. Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle

object_types.name: FeatureBundleName
object_types.definition: Unique name of a feature bundle, e.g. Starter, Professional, Enterprise.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product; identified by subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.
Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription ends; optional, present only for fixed-term or cancelled subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. ... A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: Status of a subscription; one of trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused; not part of the status enumeration but overlaps with it.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with an effective date and requester; the change history that a subscription's current plan is derived from.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date ... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a plan change record.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: Date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester

ambiguities.description: The subscription-plan relationship is stated twice inconsistently: the read-back says a subscription 'belongs to exactly one price plan' (a direct fact), but Priya/Sam clarify there is also a full change history (PlanChange records) from which the current plan is derived, plus a denormalized 'current plan' field maintained by the change process. Is the direct Subscription-PricePlan fact type the authoritative current-plan link (maintained by the change process, described as 'denormalised'), or should the model only expose PlanChange history and derive current plan via query? The two representations could drift ('if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug').

source_references.excerpt: No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record. ... if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: Three distinct concepts are all called 'plan': the billing artefact (PricePlan), the feature bundle (FeatureBundle), and a third thing sales calls a plan (the negotiated deal), which was explicitly not discussed further ('that's a different meeting'). Should the negotiated sales deal be modeled as yet another entity, and how does it relate to PricePlan/FeatureBundle?

source_references.excerpt: We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither. ... Don't. That's a different meeting.

ambiguities.description: The 'one active subscription per account per product' rule is clear, but the exact uniqueness scope (is it uniqueness only among subscriptions with status 'active', or does it also constrain 'trialing'/other statuses?) is not fully specified. This affects whether the external uniqueness constraint should be conditioned on status.

source_references.excerpt: One active subscription. ... One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level.

ambiguities.description: The commercial policy for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term vs prorated refund vs credit) is explicitly undecided and parked by the facilitator. The model captures only the system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund mechanism), but the business rule is unresolved and manual credits are being issued outside the modeled system.

source_references.excerpt: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Tom mentions a fourth product 'in discovery' with an unknown identifier/shape. Should the Product value_constraint (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) be treated as closed, or is it expected to expand soon, making a fixed value_constraint premature?

source_references.excerpt: Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: PausedFlag is described as a separate boolean that overlaps confusingly with SubscriptionStatus (a paused subscription might still show as 'active' status). No constraint was given for how PausedFlag interacts with SubscriptionStatus (e.g., can only active subscriptions be paused?). This interaction needs clarification to avoid modeling an incomplete/inconsistent rule.

source_references.excerpt: It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: Tom argues that account number resets to a new account when a company closes and reopens, losing history from a product perspective, but this is affirmed as the deliberate finance rule. It's unclear whether any cross-account linkage (e.g., 'same company, new account') should be modeled at all, since it's explicitly rejected for reporting but desired by product.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... It drives finance the other way.
